requirements.evidence: Catalog, adapters, skills, persistence and platform checks preserved; the plugin was extended in place across commits fcb79ea..2e27e2a rather than recreated.

Tool identity is now independent of model identity: a catalog `contract` binding decides the tool name, the host registers ONE tool per contract, and a two-implementation catalog test proves two models yield one `lang_detect`. Adapter factories are now keyed on the npm PACKAGE rather than the model id, because keying on the id was itself a model-name switch that made a second conforming implementation unservable. Provider override is host config with documented fallback. Remaining: the merge is proven with test fixtures, not with two distinct real models.

`stt_transcribe` is now the canonical registered name and `transcribe_audio` is an opt-in alias (`legacyAliases`, default false) so it stays out of the default catalog. Tests assert the alias is absent by default, appears only when enabled, and keeps its own argument shape (`audio_path`) rather than being reinterpreted as the canonical contract's (`audio.path`). Remaining: not exercised against a real recording.

Explicit requiredness comes from the contract schema required array; parameter-order inference is gone from the contract path. Real per-tool output schemas are enforced by Ajv on every result. DSH cannot advertise every JSON-Schema keyword, so the projection reports what it omits and argument validation enforces it against the untouched contract (tested: minLength is reported as runtime-enforced and still rejects a short value). Remaining: the legacy per-model registrar path still infers requiredness from parameter order.

The host now constructs an InvocationAuthority from an operator-built grant and passes it to every adapter, so a request cannot supply or widen it. It carries grantId, caller kind, limits, recording policy and a resolvePath bound to the approved roots; a test asserts the object exposes no mutable roots list. SEC-03 tool grants and SEC-10 destination grants are enforced before inference. Remaining: filesystem access is wired into the Voz path tool but not every adapter, and the harness-executor/capability fields of SEC-03 do not exist yet.

The host holds no model-specific code, and the property is now ENFORCED rather than inspected. `npm run verify:architecture` fails the build on three shapes of a private built-in path: a vendor SDK import, a branch on a literal model id, and a non-empty ADAPTER_FACTORIES. The rules match SHAPE rather than a list of known model names, because a rule enumerating today's models would pass the day a new one is added, which is exactly when it must fail. PROVEN TO FIRE: the gate was run against the real code this repository shipped before the extraction (the `entry.id === 'tongue'` branch in registrar.ts, the two-entry ADAPTER_FACTORIES list, the vendor import) and rejects all three, and re-introducing the registrar branch into the working tree fails the gate with the offending file and line. It distinguishes configuration from a built-in: comparing against an operator-configured provider override is accepted, the same shape written with a literal is rejected, and comments documenting a prohibition do not satisfy it. Both extraction requirements are satisfied: model implementations live in independently versioned packages reached only through the public extension API, and both packages are built and linked.

DISPATCH AUTHORITY IS NOW ENFORCED BY A GATE rather than asserted. The architecture check fails the build when the MCP or dispatch layers call a tool DEFINITION execute - including a ctx.tools.get() whose execute would bypass the pipeline - and the rule distinguishes the receiver, because that is what separates an authority from a bypass. The existing path was already correct: the MCP binding dispatches through an INJECTED executor, which index.ts supplies as ctx.tools.execute. A test asserts both directions - that definition.execute is flagged and that an injected surface.execute is accepted, since treating dependency injection as a bypass produced a false positive. Remaining: Code Mode does not exist, so the rule is enforced over the MCP layer only and its application to a future Code Mode path is unproven.

One installable host bundle exists (packages/dsh-model-as-tool with its cordis patch), and every model/tool extension is a SEPARATE package with its own version. RELEASE INDEPENDENCE IS NOW CHECKED: a gate fails the build if any extension declares the host package in dependencies, peerDependencies or optionalDependencies, because that would couple the extension to a host release and make "installing one extension must not require rebuilding the host" false. A test asserts the property holds today and that the check fires on a fixture that violates it. Remaining: no single bundle TARBALL is built that installs the host plus its declared peers, and the bundles are not versioned as one artefact, so "one installable bundle" is satisfied structurally rather than as a shipped artifact. The extensions are not published to npm either.

The responsibility partition holds in the code: the host owns the MCP listener lifecycle, the export policy, external caller contexts, extension installation and activation, deployment coordination and contribution projection; the extensions own their adapters, assets, recipes and skills, and the architecture gate proves no model-specific implementation lives in the host. Reuse of DSH contracts is real where it fits: dispatch goes through ctx.tools.execute, skills through the DSH skill registry, and the tools themselves are registered through the DSH tool registry rather than a parallel one. Remaining: there is no MODEL PREPARATION surface on the host (plans are computed but never produced), no managed-process usage because there is no worker runtime, and no PTC runtime integration because Code Mode does not exist. The partition is therefore correct in what it assigns and incomplete in what it operates.

NOT IMPLEMENTED, and the parts that exist are worth distinguishing from it. The SAFELY KEYED POOL mechanism the requirement asks for does exist: DeploymentCoordinator keys a deployment by extension, model, revision, engine version, quantization, tokenizer and preprocessing recipe, so a Voz extension running headlessly would share one instance rather than starting a second merely because an MCP client connected - and single-flight is asserted by counting loader invocations. The headless requirement is also satisfied: the Voz extension takes a FILE PATH and performs path authorization before opening anything, so no microphone or browser UI is required for headless transcription. What does NOT exist is the documented public bridge for REUSING a registered DSH speechToText provider. Nothing discovers a provider DSH already has, so a host that already holds a Voz instance would start its own.

There is ONE execution path. The MCP surface does not implement its own executor: the host binding resolves a tool and dispatches through ctx.tools.execute, so validation, grants, receipts and result policy are applied by the same pipeline a native call uses, and a gate now fails the build if a second path appears. The shared metadata and catalog layer the requirement permits does exist: contracts carry the canonical schemas, the publication surface decides what may be advertised, and the MCP descriptor is derived from the contract rather than restated. Remaining: no worker transport exists, which the requirement explicitly permits as an alternative to a parallel dispatch path, so the permitted option is simply absent rather than chosen.

NO EXTENSION RECEIVES RAW DSH CONTEXT, by construction rather than by convention: ExtensionContextV1 carries host-issued identity, private storage, a bounded logger and a teardown signal, and has NO DSH ctx member, no registry mutation, no global credentials and no unfiltered environment. The architecture gate separately proves no extension imports DSH or the host. NO HARDCODED MODEL-SPECIFIC PROMPT, now checked by a gate. The rule needed REFINING and the refinement is the interesting part: the first version flagged three things that were not prompts - an error message mentioning transcription, a parameter description naming example model ids, and a warning template - because it tested for length rather than for instruction phrasing. It now requires imperative phrasing naming a model, and tests assert it catches "You are a transcription assistant..." while accepting all three false positives. A gate with false positives is worse than a narrow one, because it teaches its reader to skip it. The host validating declarations and creating its own registry wrappers is real: registration goes through defineTool and the host owns the wrapper, so an extension never registers into DSH directly. Remaining: declarative extensions have no interpreter, so the generic host-owned recipe path described here does not exist; and there is no managed runtime for a wrapper to dispatch into.

The MCP listener lifecycle is a SEPARATE object from the plugin registration state, which is what makes the requirement satisfiable: disabling the server stops its listener and its owned work, and a test asserts it does not disable unrelated DSH tools, because the two are independently stoppable rather than one flag. Remaining: there is no configuration switch that enables or disables MCP export from the plugin, so the separate lifecycle exists but nothing wires it to a setting; and disabling the whole plugin relies on Cordis effect disposal, which releases registrations but has not been exercised against a running listener.

The listener is a Node HTTP listener owned by the plugin effect, built on node:http rather than on a DSH route, so no upstream DSH patch is required to open an MCP endpoint - which is what the requirement asks for. It is not SDK-backed, and cannot be: the published SDK does not support revision 2026-07-28, so the listener is a schema-conformant adaptation under MCP-01. The requirement prefers an SDK-backed listener, and the honest position is that the SDK cannot be the basis for this revision yet. Remaining: DSH route reuse was not evaluated, because no documented DSH route API with the necessary lifecycle and transport behaviour was found; if one exists, reusing it would be preferable to a second listener.
No headless launcher exists. Nothing boots a minimal DSH composition with the Tool Mode host and MCP export enabled, so there is no launch path for a user without an interactive DSH session.

No package binary for launching the server is declared. The operator CLI (dsh-tool-mode) and the stdio bridge (dsh-tool-mode-mcp-stdio) exist, but neither starts a listener, and no command documented for that purpose exists.

A startup policy type encodes the prohibition rather than leaving it to a comment: preparesModels and resolvesPackages are FALSE literals in the type, so a caller cannot construct a policy that permits them, and startupPermits refuses prepare-model, resolve-package and download-weights while permitting restore-active, inspect-assets and read-manifests. Discovery is genuinely static and read-only: discoverExtension reads package.json and the manifest as BOUNDED DATA and imports nothing, which is asserted by a test whose fixture ships an entry that THROWS on import. Remaining: nothing is RESTORED at startup, because there is no profile store and no activation surface to restore from; and the startup path is a policy with no caller, so the prohibition is enforced where it is consulted and nothing consults it yet.

READINESS IS A DERIVED STATE, not a flag: it is true only after BOTH bind and initialisation succeeded, and the observable event order is asserted as bind, initialise, ready. A bind that fails never reaches initialise, and an initialisation that fails CLOSES the bound listener rather than leaving a port that answers nothing. A PORT CONFLICT IS REPORTED, NOT RESOLVED. EADDRINUSE returns PORT_IN_USE with a remedy naming both forbidden resolutions in as many words - the server will not take the port by force or move silently - and the lifecycle reports no port at all after a conflict, so nothing can relocate without saying so. A FAILED START CANNOT CRASH THE HOST, asserted across all three failure modes: the result is RETURNED rather than thrown, which is the difference between one feature being unavailable and the host going down. Remaining: the listener is not actually started from the plugin, so these behaviours are exercised against a synthetic host; and the HTTP server factory does not yet route its bind failure through this lifecycle.

THE ORDER IS THE REQUIREMENT ORDER and is asserted: refuse new work, cancel owned foreground invocations, wait within a DOCUMENTED grace period, terminate what remains, close the transport and release the port. Work adopted during the shutdown window is REFUSED, because it would otherwise be left running. WORK THAT OUTLIVES THE GRACE PERIOD IS TERMINATED AND REPORTED AS SUCH - a test holds a cancel that never resolves and asserts it appears in terminated rather than cancelled, and that withinGrace is false. A cancel that hangs must not hold shutdown open forever, nor be reported as stopped. WORK BELONGING TO ANOTHER OWNER IS NEVER TOUCHED. A test adopts work for two owners, stops as one, and asserts the other is neither cancelled nor terminated and is reported as untouched, because a model process serving another still-authorized owner is not this lifecycle to kill. Remaining: the grace period is asserted against a synthetic host and no real process is terminated, because there is no managed worker runtime; and no registrations are removed because the lifecycle is not yet wired to the plugin registration state.

THE PUBLISHED HOST IS INSTALLABLE AND CORRECT. @try-works/dsh-model-as-tool@0.1.3 is on the public registry, and a ground-truth install into a clean directory succeeds: 35 packages, the bundled contracts resolves from within the host with its 16 exports, and the host carries 21 modules plus 6 in the MCP layer with no tongue.js and no voz.js - so BASE-09 holds of the artifact a consumer actually receives. A CORRECTION, AND THE SAME ONE TWICE. I previously reported that @try-works/tool-mode-contracts was never published and that publishes were being silently dropped. BOTH WERE WRONG. Contracts IS published at 0.1.0, and the earlier 404s were read before propagation finished - a registry read taken immediately after a publish is not evidence in EITHER direction, and I over-concluded from a negative result twice. The bundle remains worthwhile because it removes a runtime dependency on a second package, but it was not the fix I claimed: publishing contracts was. THE REAL BLOCKER FOR THE EXTENSIONS WAS `private: true`, which I had set and which silently prevents publication. It is removed, and the extension SDK and both extension packages were published this round. ALL THREE ARE NOW CONFIRMED PUBLISHED on a DEFERRED registry read: the extension SDK, tongue and voz are each at 0.1.0. A consumer install of the tongue extension from the registry succeeds - 8 packages - and the installed manifest carries its five licence layers, its network declaration and its built lib/index.js, so the licensing work is exercised by an artifact a consumer actually receives and not merely by the repository. Remaining: no Windows installation of an EXTENSION from the registry has been performed specifically, and the two extensions are not yet loadable by the host end to end, because the host resolves extensions from a configured directory rather than from node_modules. Windows installation from the registry has been exercised only for the host.

A schema-conformant adaptation of revision 2026-07-28 exists, and conformance is now VERIFIED AGAINST THE PINNED UPSTREAM SCHEMA rather than against a reading of the prose. The official schema.json, schema.ts and schema.mdx are pinned under docs/tool-mode/specs/mcp-2026-07-28/ at commit 5f5440bb26a62e2cf3440b92da5a667efa03b267 (resolved from the 2026-07-28 tag, so the pin is immutable rather than a moving ref), with SHA-256 digests asserted by test so a later edit to the pinned copy is detected. It is a self-contained 2020-12 schema with no remote $ref, checked by test. Pinning immediately found THREE REAL CONFORMANCE ERRORS in code that had passed every hand-written test: a DiscoverResult carrying three fields the definition does not declare and NONE of the five it requires; a ListToolsResult missing cacheScope and ttlMs, which the definition requires; and a metadata parser requiring clientInfo where the schema makes it optional, so it rejected requests the schema admits. All three are fixed and every message the server sends is now validated against the pinned definitions by Ajv (DiscoverResultResponse, ListToolsResultResponse, CallToolResultResponse for both success and tool-error, JSONRPCErrorResponse, HeaderMismatchError). Remaining: the HTTP transport, SSE response channel, subscriptions/listen, normalised cancellation and the stdio bridge executable do not exist; the protocol/client compatibility matrix is not yet recorded as a released artifact. ADDED AFTER ADVERSARIAL REVIEW: an earlier note in this repository claimed the published SDK "cannot speak revision 2026-07-28". That was true of the V1 LINE ONLY — @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32.1 caps at 2025-11-25 — and it is corrected. The V2 line, @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.3.1, DOES implement the revision: it exports DiscoverRequestSchema, DiscoverResultSchema and PROTOCOL_VERSION_META_KEY, and the server package source serves the 2026-07-28 protocol revision. The official client was then driven against THIS server over a real socket: with versionNegotiation mode "auto" it probes with server/discover, connects, lists tools, and runs REAL inference through tools/call (lang_detect on German returns de) and is refused without a credential — 6 tests, 0 skipped. A default-configured client still negotiates initialize at 2025-11-25 and never probes, which is why the modern era is OPT-IN and why this server answers -32601 to that handshake; both halves are asserted. STILL PARTIAL because the subscription acknowledgement is produced and read by no transport.

The loopback HTTP endpoint exists and is proven to bind and serve a real request over a real socket: startHttpServer refuses a non-loopback bind address AT STARTUP rather than warning and binding anyway, which is the only enforcement that cannot be forgotten later, and it listens on the loopback interface specifically rather than on all interfaces. The path, port and body limit are configurable, defaulting to /mcp, 3765 and 4 MiB. The handler is a pure function of a request description, so every refusal path is testable without a port. Remaining: no TLS (loopback only, so none is needed), and LAN/public binding is out of scope for the first release as the requirement states.

The stdio bridge exists as a library (src/mcp/stdio.ts) and an executable (bin/dsh-tool-mode-mcp-stdio.mjs), and per P26-05 it is an HTTP CLIENT rather than a second protocol implementation: it generates the modern per-request headers and posts to the same endpoint a network client uses, so there is no second interpretation of the protocol to drift out of step. Two simultaneous authorized clients with independently revocable credentials are proven against one host surface, and a client credential is refused by another client endpoint. Remain: the stdout-purity property of the executable is verified STATICALLY rather than by running it, because this sandbox cannot spawn a child with piped stdio (named pipes are blocked); the check asserts there are exactly two stdout writes and that both are protocol frames, that every diagnostic goes through a named stderr sink, and that console.log does not appear at all. That is weaker than an end-to-end run and is recorded as such.

A modern tools/list and tools/call are proven to be processable as the FIRST application request with no initialize handshake and no session, because the dispatch layer is stateless by construction. Evidence is now an artifact rather than an assertion: the fixture corpus captures both as first requests, and the independently-authored probe validates them against the pinned upstream schema. The COMPATIBILITY MATRIX is recorded in docs/tool-mode/fixtures/mcp-2026-07-28/MANIFEST.json: the exact revision, the pinned schema commit, the official SDK version, and the fact that the SDK does NOT support this revision, so this server is the schema-conformant adaptation MCP-01 permits rather than an SDK configuration. Remaining: the SDK version currently reads not-installed because the official SDK is not a dependency of this repository, so the matrix records its absence rather than a version. No legacy translation mode is offered or tested. A report asserting only a 2026-07-28 string equality would still fail the gate, which is why the probe asserts schema conformance of actual message bodies per fixture instead.

server/discover returns the revision, the server identity and the full feature matrix including what is NOT implemented, so a client can distinguish absent from unmentioned. Tool discovery and invocation are implemented with deterministic ordering and a JSON-RPC error for an unknown method rather than a pretence of service. Remaining: authorized catalog subscriptions (subscriptions/listen), transport-specific cancellation, and the HTTP endpoint itself are not implemented.

tools/list is deterministically ordered (asserted), and the surface lists what the host reports as authorized rather than a global catalog. The publication surface already withholds a tool whose selected implementation is not callable and reports readiness instead (EXT-24), so an unprepared catalog entry does not become an inference leaf. Remaining: the caller-permitted set is not yet computed per grant at the MCP boundary, and the requirement that installed-but-cold models count as callable is not exercised because there is no preparation lifecycle.

The MCP surface is now bound to the real registry: a new mcp/host-binding.ts builds the surface over the contracts the activation actually REGISTERED, so it cannot advertise a tool the publication surface withheld, and invocation is routed through the DSH tool runtime ctx.tools.execute(). A test asserts the SERVER-ISSUED call identity reaches the executor and that a distinct one is issued per invocation, because a caller-supplied identity would let a caller forge a receipt, and it asserts the executor receives the CALLER OWN signal so cancellation reaches the actual work. A host failure is reported as a tool error rather than a fabricated success. Remaining: no test drives a full tools/call through dispatch into a real inference call, because the models this host can run are not prepared; the caller-permitted set is not computed per grant at the MCP boundary; and native input validation is the contract validation already applied by the registered tool body rather than a separate MCP-side check.

The canonical OUTPUT schema is exported, and the provenance is asserted rather than assumed: derivePayloadSchema removes ONLY the reserved root meta property and its required entry, per the section 16.4 derivation, and tests prove every other property and constraint survives verbatim and that the derivation does not mutate the shared contract. Both schemas come from the CONTRACTS, never from DSH model-facing schemas() projection, which intentionally omits output. The fact is observable through the control tool: a new read-only mcp action reports each exported tool and whether it has an output schema, with a test asserting every one does, and another asserting the exported set EQUALS the registered set, so MCP cannot advertise something the host withheld. Remaining: the schemas are exported but no client has been driven against them end to end, and a tool that is registered but whose model is unprepared still appears, because the publication surface treats a runnable model as ready in the absence of a preparation lifecycle.

The finalized canonical value is returned in structuredContent with a bounded model-readable content rendering, and the two error kinds are kept distinct in both directions, each with a test: an application failure is a SUCCESSFUL protocol response carrying isError with resultType complete, while an infrastructure failure, an unknown tool and malformed arguments are JSON-RPC errors with no result member. An unknown tool is deliberately invalid params rather than a tool error, because nothing was invoked and a domain failure would be a fabrication. Remaining: the bounded content rendering is a plain text projection rather than a content-block policy, and the post-policy canonical value is whatever the host returns, since no result policy layer exists yet.

A tool that cannot be exported faithfully is withheld ENTIRELY with a recorded reason rather than partly serialized, and onWithheld reports it so the reason is not lost. Writing the tests found a real bug in this: callTool looked for the tool in the published set, which INCLUDES withheld tools, so a client that guessed the name could invoke exactly the tool the export deliberately refused to promise - defeating the requirement through the back door. It now checks exportability as well as presence, and a test covers it. Remaining: nothing yet produces a notExportableReason, so the path is exercised against a fixture rather than by a real non-exportable host tool; TMX extension tools are not yet routed through this same mapping.

A tool whose definition reports importedFromMcp is refused at dispatch with invalid params and never invoked, asserted by a test that also checks the host was not called, because re-exporting would let a server delegate back into itself through a loop no caller can see. Remaining: nothing yet produces an imported MCP tool, so the guard is exercised against a stub rather than against a real import path.

All five named controls are implemented and tested: the LOOPBACK check reads the socket address rather than a caller-supplied header, because trusting a header would make the binding decorative; Host is therefore not the check; approved ORIGINS are an allow-list and an unapproved browser origin is refused while a request with no Origin is admitted, which is the non-browser case; request SIZE is limited and the limit is enforced DURING the read rather than after it, since buffering an unbounded body to measure it defeats the limit; and AUTHENTICATION is required on every request including discovery, with the token compared in constant time and never echoed in a failure response. CORS is not authentication, proven by a test where an approved origin with a bad token still returns 401. Remaining: the OAuth 2.1 resource-server profile is not implemented, so audience and scope validation do not exist.

createGrant models allowedTools, approvedRoots, remoteDestinations, hostedCode, recordingPolicy and limits; authorizeTool/authorizeDestination refuse before any model work. Defaults are conservative (no hosted code, no recording, no roots, so it fails closed). Remaining: per-application independently revocable credentials (SEC-01) and harness-executor profiles are not implemented, and the interactive grant covers the standard tools rather than being created per client.

authorizePath resolves drive letters, separators, Unicode, junctions and symlinks via realpathSync.native, then checks containment on a separator boundary; it refuses relative paths, UNC and Windows device paths, NUL bytes, missing paths and anything outside every root, and returns the CANONICAL path so the caller opens what was authorized rather than re-resolving it (closing the check-then-open race). Tested against real directories and real Windows junctions, including Unicode and space-containing valid paths, a sibling whose name shares a prefix, traversal, and links that stay inside. 1 of 24 cases skipped where the platform forbids file symlinks without elevation; the equivalent junction case covers that escape.

authorizeDestination refuses an unauthorized remote destination, and the grant exposes no silent local-to-remote fallback path. Remaining: the hosted-code and harness-executor edges of the rule are not implemented.

Each release tool IS authored once as a model-free contract carrying identity, version, input and output schema, semantics, limits, unsupported cases and implementation bindings, and DSH registration and the MCP projection are both GENERATED from that one source rather than restated. Remaining: examples are not part of the contract shape, so the author-once source is incomplete against the requirement list; Code Mode type generation does not exist because Code Mode does not; and policy metadata beyond limits and unsupported cases is not modelled.

THE REQUIREMENT IS RIGHT AND THIS REPOSITORY CANNOT YET SATISFY IT, and that is worth recording precisely rather than leaving as a gap somebody re-attempts. DECL-02 says an unconstrained {type: object, additionalProperties: true} is not an adequate implementation of an ordinary leaf tool contract. The registered contract tools still carry exactly that for their OUTPUT, because the contract real output schema cannot be projected into DSH value-schema DSL. Four distinct rejections were hit at registration, each recorded in the code: (1) schema.required is not supported; (2) schema.properties.candidates.items.required is not supported, so required is unsupported at EVERY depth and not merely at the root; (3) schema.properties.words.items is not supported, and items is in the documented supported set, so its support does not extend to an array nested inside an object, which is what every output schema contains; (4) schema.properties.reliability.enum must be a non-empty array of scalar values, and expressing the union type as oneOf was rejected too with oneOf must be an array of at least two value schemas. Stripping each keyword in turn DOES converge, and converging was rejected deliberately: it produces a schema that advertises almost nothing while APPEARING to be a real declaration, which is worse than the open object because a client would trust it. The contract itself is unchanged and complete, and assertValidOutput enforces the real schema at runtime against the untouched contract, so RESULTS ARE VALIDATED - what is missing is the ADVERTISEMENT. What does hold: the INPUT schema projection is genuine and complete, with real requiredness, nesting, units and limits, and every keyword the DSL cannot express is returned in runtimeEnforced and checked at runtime rather than silently discarded, which is what BASE-04 requires. Remaining: the output advertisement, blocked on the DSL limitation above. Publishing the real output schema requires either a DSH DSL that supports nested items, deep required and non-scalar enums, or a different advertisement channel.

The shared result metadata exists and is stamped by the HOST, not the extension: contractVersion, implementationId, extension identity with version and digest, executionLocation, receiptId and warnings. A test asserts an extension supplying its own reserved root meta is refused, because an extension asserting its own provenance is exactly what this forbids. Model identity stays accessible through the implementation binding without requiring the agent to select a model, which is the second half of the requirement. Remaining: the metadata structure is not carried as a SCHEMA inside each tool contract, which the requirement asks for so a client can discover the envelope shape. It is defined once in code and applied by the host, so the substance holds and the discoverable schema does not.

Confidence is not fabricated. The detector reports the VENDOR-REPORTED reliability the model itself produces and names its source, so a caller can tell a vendor claim from a calibrated estimate, and there is no generic confidence number invented by the host. A successful call is reported as a valid result rather than a correct one: the contract semantics state that a produced result means the pipeline succeeded. Remaining: only two of the four categories the requirement names are representable - vendor-reported and unavailable are, while independently calibrated estimates and ranking logits are not modelled because no implementation produces them. The confidence distinction is also not carried in the output SCHEMA, for the same projection reason as DECL-02.

Tools and skills are registered with concise descriptions, supported inputs, unsupported cases and data-handling notes, generated from the contract so the description cannot drift from the schema. Skills are registered through the DSH skill provider as GUIDANCE, carrying no executable registration and granting no permission. Remaining: native and Code Mode examples are not part of the contract, so the example half of the requirement is unmet; recovery advice is not modelled as a field; and the skill text does not yet carry per-tool unsupported cases through from the contract.

Catalog changes are applied at coherent boundaries: registration and unregistration happen through extension activation and deactivation rather than mid-request, and publication is atomic - the whole surface is built and validated before any of it is swapped in, so a client never observes a half-updated catalog. Nothing rewrites history, manufactures user tasks or inserts tool results into the composer: a foreground tool returns through its tool-result channel, and the MCP layer only ever responds to a request. Remaining: no notification is emitted when the catalog changes, so a connected client learns of a change only by asking; coherence is achieved by atomicity rather than by announcing the transition.

A read-only control surface exists and is registered as the model_tools tool, exposing catalog discovery, per-model describe, enable/disable and reset, and it is reachable to authorized callers through the same governed pipeline as any other tool rather than through a private path. Remaining: the surface is registered as a DSH tool and is therefore available to native callers, but it is NOT exposed over MCP, so an external caller cannot read it; and the enable/disable state it reports is process-local rather than persisted, which was a deliberate earlier decision and is a divergence from what an external caller would expect.

Contributions carry their owning extension and activation generation, and the host stamps authoritative identity so a package cannot claim another provenance. Host control tools such as discovery and composition remain host-owned and are not supplied by a model package, which the architecture gate enforces by refusing model-specific code in the host. An old generated binding cannot bypass current activation or permissions, because admission is evaluated per invocation from the live extension state rather than cached in the binding - the readiness correction in RES-04 hardened exactly this path. Remaining: recipe digest is not carried on a contribution, because there is no recipe concept; and per-package and per-tool revocation is not implemented at all, so coherent reflection of a revocation across every surface has nothing to reflect yet.

The EmbeddingGemma 2 identity is recorded as the model card describes it: version 2, a modular 740M model supporting text, code, images, audio and video in a SHARED embedding space, with 768-dimensional embeddings reducible to 512, 256 and 128. The reduced widths are asserted as a set rather than inferred, because a reduction applied inconsistently produces vectors that cannot be compared with each other. The substitution rule is enforced: an embedding space may stand in for another only when the DIMENSIONS MATCH, and the refusal names BOTH widths. EmbeddingGemma 2 at 768 replacing MiniLM at 384 is refused, with the description stating that existing vectors are not comparable and require an explicit re-index - because comparing different-width vectors produces meaningless similarity rather than an error. Remaining: NO EmbeddingGemma 2 IMPLEMENTATION EXISTS. Nothing downloads it, converts it, quantizes it or runs it, so the runtime and artifact manifest the requirement asks for does not exist and the exact conversion, quantization and preprocessing are unrecorded because there is no artifact to describe. The identity is modelled; the model is absent.

BLOCKED ON A MISSING PUBLISHED PACKAGE, verified earlier and re-checked: npm `laya-ts` returns 404, so there is no published Node entry point for the Laya decision model. Without it the local implementation cannot use Laya actual trained decision heads and tokenizer/config, which is what the requirement demands rather than a replacement chat prompt. What IS recorded and enforced: an embedding-based label scorer is a different contract from the probabilistic decision contract, and the contract registry has no decision contract registered at all - so the mis-mapping the requirement warns about cannot occur, because nothing implements it. Jev is recorded as an explicitly remote alternative rather than a local one. Remaining: everything the requirement asks for, pending a published Laya package.

BLOCKED ON A MISSING NODE DISTRIBUTION, verified earlier: Needle exists (github.com/cactus-compute/needle) but no verified Node or WASM distribution for Needle 3 was found, so it cannot be executed under the execution modes MODEL-04 permits. What IS enforced is the prohibition the requirement names: nothing advertises Needle as a general-purpose instruction or chat model, and nothing uses an autonomous execute/run helper to dispatch DSH tools, because there is no Needle adapter to do either. The bounded proposal/extraction shape the requirement asks for is the shape the contract registry would require. Remaining: everything the requirement asks for, pending a verified Node distribution.

requirements.summary: Prefer Node-compatible execution, not JavaScript-only weights.
requirements.evidence: The permitted and refused execution modes are encoded and each refusal carries a reason: pure JS/WASM usable in plain Node, prebuilt ONNX Runtime for Node and a managed native Windows executable are ACCEPTED; Python-required, WSL-required, Docker-required, GPU-required, browser-only and consumer-compile are all REFUSED. The Python distinction the requirement draws is preserved rather than flattened: the refusal says Python may be used by MAINTAINERS to export and verify artifacts but must not be required on an end user machine. A browser-only API is refused with the reason the requirement gives - it does not establish Node support. The only two runnable implementations satisfy this in fact: Tongue is pure JavaScript needing no runtime, and Voz uses prebuilt ONNX Runtime for Node. No consumer compile, WSL, Docker or GPU is required by either. Remaining: nothing CHECKS an extension against these modes at install or activation time, so the verdict is computable and unconsulted, and a future extension declaring a refused mode would not be stopped by the host.

A QUALIFICATION RECORD requires all eight fields the requirement names - model revision, exported artifact SHA, tokenizer, processor, engine and package version, Node ABI, architecture and execution provider - and reports EVERY missing field rather than the first, so one pass tells a maintainer everything left to record. An empty string counts as MISSING rather than as recorded, because a field present but blank is a gap wearing the shape of an answer. The rule that a platform table, a successful package import or a runnable base model is NOT proof of correct inference is enforced structurally: those are not fields of the record, so none of them can satisfy it. DISCOVERY DESCRIBES THE INTERSECTION. A model can support a modality while the selected adapter does not, so the advertisable set is the intersection of the two, and the description NAMES the model-only modalities rather than omitting them - a reader must not be left to infer that the model lacks video when in fact the adapter does. Remaining: no real model has a qualification record, because the two runnable implementations do not publish one, so the record is enforced by test and unpopulated in practice. There are no real Windows CPU tests for the adapters, which the requirement demands, and no adapter support is declared anywhere for an intersection to be computed from.

Capability resolves to THREE DISTINCT STATES - supported, unsupported and unknown - and a test asserts the set has three members rather than two, because the requirement says to record unknown and unsupported SEPARATELY and collapsing them lets an unevaluated capability be reported as a known absence. An unevaluated capability is NOT inferred from a sibling: text support says nothing about video support, so an unobserved video capability stays unknown however well text performs. A MODEL NAME IS NEVER A CAPABILITY TEST. modelNameImpliesCapability returns false so the prohibition is asserted rather than merely intended, since a rule that lives only in a comment is one a future branch will not read. Remaining: the resolver is not wired to a real DSH provider, so the current provider and model are not actually resolved through DSH as the requirement asks; nothing records which provider was current for a past decision; and adding a compatible DSH provider has not been demonstrated to need no recipe change, because there are no recipes.

PARTIAL COVERAGE IS REPORTED AND AN INCOMPLETE CLIP IS NOT PRESENTED AS FULLY TRANSCRIBED: a transcript whose coverage is incomplete is rendered with an explicit warning naming the seconds covered, which is the half of the requirement that matters most for correctness. An empty transcript is a valid empty transcript rather than an error, reported as "no speech recognized", which is the opposite of the title rule and deliberately so - silence is a real result, whereas a refusal is not. Remaining: the format is not INSPECTED. The requirement says to check sample count and format rather than the file extension alone, and the implementation validates the path and its authorization but not the header, so a 44.1 kHz stereo file would not be refused as unsupported; there is no bounded tested decoder for additional encodings, so they are simply unsupported; unsupported requested timestamps are not modelled as errors at all; and the model lower contextual and admission limits are not consulted against the source-file defaults.

BLOCKED ON THE SAME MISSING PACKAGE AS MODEL-02: npm `laya-ts` returns 404, so Laya typed prediction API is unobtainable and the requirement to use it rather than constrained chat generation cannot be met. The alternative the requirement explicitly rules out - an embedding-based label scorer standing in for the probabilistic decision contract - is therefore correctly NOT implemented, since implementing it would be the defect rather than the fix. Remaining: the whole contract. No decision tool is registered, so there is no choice-set validation, no abstention policy and no Jev mapping to get wrong.

THE REQUIREMENT NAMES A MISTAKE THAT IS EASY TO MAKE - a text language detector exists, audio exists, and the two look combinable. The rule is now enforced: a result that examined TEXT is not evidence about the language spoken in AUDIO, asserted per medium rather than per result, because the result itself is sound and only its use as audio evidence is not. The description a text result carries says so in as many words - that it is the language of the supplied text and not evidence of the language spoken in audio - so the disclosure travels with the result rather than relying on a caller to remember. The existing lang_detect contract already preserves ambiguity and empty-input handling by returning ranked candidates rather than a single forced answer, and reports a vendor-supplied score rather than a calibrated probability. Remaining: the rule is not attached to the registered lang_detect tool, so its description does not yet carry the disclosure an agent would read; and no audio language path exists to make the distinction concrete.

The one rule that can be enforced without an embedding implementation IS enforced: an embedding space may stand in for another only when the dimensions match, and changing models requires an explicit re-index. That covers the requirement to PIN an existing persistent index to its precise embedding space. Remaining: there is no MiniLM implementation, so pooling, normalization, input order, vector dimension and model identity are not preserved because there is nothing that produces them; no vector is validated for finiteness; and no persistent index exists to pin. The richer section-17 contracts the requirement says new multimodal work should use are exactly what MODEL-01 models and cannot yet run.

No cross-encoder reranking tool exists in any form: no pair scoring, no deterministic tie handling, no score-kind reporting, and no top_k validation. The MODEL-05 capability machinery would describe such a tool correctly but nothing implements it.

THE RULE THE REQUIREMENT STATES MOST SHARPLY IS ENFORCED FIRST: a refusal or an incomplete generation becomes an ERROR and never a valid empty title. This is the failure most worth preventing because it is easy to ship and hard to notice - `{ title: "" }` has the correct SHAPE, so a caller writing it into a document produces a blank heading rather than an exception, and nothing in the pipeline looks wrong. A test asserts a refusal outcome carries no title field at all, and the refusal is checked BEFORE the empty-title path so it cannot fall through to it by carrying an empty title alongside. NO INVENTED FACTS IS CHECKED, NOT MERELY REQUESTED. A number in a proposed title or description that does not appear in the source is a claim the source does not support - "10 Ways to Configure the Deployment Pipeline" over a source that never says ten is exactly the embellishment a summariser invents. The check is a provenance comparison and it rejects with the offending number named. NO CHANGED SOURCE MEANING is enforced as a real overlap requirement: a title sharing no content word with its source is not a title FOR that source but a different claim wearing the shape of one, and it is rejected. The rule abstains when the source has no content words, so a degenerate source does not cause everything to be rejected. Maximum title and description lengths are stated IN THE CONTRACT rather than chosen per call, over-length output is REJECTED rather than truncated, and repair attempts are COUNTED - with an exhausted budget reported as exhausted rather than as a failure to propose, so a caller can tell the two apart. Whether the tool may call another tool is asserted false, and the response shape carries no tool-call field for one to be dispatched from. Remaining: THE TITLE TOOL IS NOT REGISTERED. The rules exist and are tested, but no harness-text recipe package provides them and no contract is registered, so nothing an agent can call implements this. The requirement to use an INDEPENDENTLY PACKAGED recipe is therefore unmet, and the provenance checks are heuristics applied to a model response rather than a guarantee about what the model generated.

THE MANIFEST NOW DECLARES PER-LAYER LICENCES, and discovery RESOLVES them, so this is no longer a module exercised only by fixtures: both shipped extension packages declare all five layers with ZERO gaps, asserted through the same discoverExtension a host uses. A MISSING LAYER IS REPORTED AS A GAP rather than defaulted, and a package that declares no licences at all reports every layer as a gap - asserted against a synthetic silent package, because no shipped package is silent, which is the point. Both shipped packages record the weights as NOT redistributable and NOT open source, preserve the Desert Ant attribution notice in the resolved record, and keep the licence obligations readable so a deployer need not read the licence text to learn what constrains them. The conversion-artifacts layer is declared EXPLICITLY as "none: the model ships as the vendor published it" rather than left a gap, because a gap implies something missing when in fact no conversion step is performed. Remaining: the resolved record is produced by discovery but NOT persisted into an installation record; no notice file is generated or shipped, so missingNotices has nothing to check in practice; and the licence model lives in the SDK while the HOST does not yet consult it when a model is selected.

The vendor terms are declared ON REAL SHIPPED PACKAGES and asserted for both: the weights and SDK layers are marked NOT open source, named as Source-Available with a URL a reviewer can read, and carry the researched obligations including the per-platform per-model active-device threshold, the no-rehosting rule and the no-competing-model-training rule. The distinction the requirement draws - source-available, NOT open source - is asserted per package rather than stated once, because it is the fact most likely to be lost by treating a licence file presence as open-source status. Remaining: the licence is not attached to any CATALOG model, so nothing verifies at selection time that a chosen model carries these terms; the active-device threshold is recorded as an obligation but NOT counted or enforced because nothing tracks devices; and no vendor clarification has been obtained for the export-boundary question.

A permission basis is a HUMAN RECORD carrying the scope it covers, one of four basis kinds, the responsible person and the time, plus what it excludes - and there is deliberately NO config-boolean member in the type, because a type that cannot express one is a stronger guarantee than a comment saying not to use one. A runtime guard asserts a boolean, a string and an empty object are all rejected, and that an unattributed record is refused. EXPORT IS SCOPED TO THE PROVIDER: an unresolved external-export permission blocks that provider ONLY, and the refusal message says so in as many words, because one unresolved question must not disable the whole plugin. Native use and external export are separate scopes, so a native-use permission alone does not authorise export - which is the point of tracking scopes independently. Remaining: no permission record is actually recorded for any provider, so nothing is exportable today; there is no CLI or management surface to record one; and no vendor clarification or qualified review has been obtained, which is the human step the requirement asks for and which this implementation cannot perform for itself.

BOTH SHIPPED PACKAGES DECLARE THEIR NETWORK BEHAVIOUR, and the declaration is what discovery derives the verdict from: each is INELIGIBLE for a strict no-network deployment, each refusal carries a qualified alternative, and neither can be described as network-free because describeNetwork derives the description from the declaration rather than accepting one from a deployer. The telemetry declaration names WHAT the telemetry carries - a monthly active-device count generated by an SDK-generated id - which is what makes the description accurate rather than merely cautious. That matches the vendor behaviour researched earlier: a minimal active-device count carrying no inputs, outputs or content. A package declaring NOTHING is treated as TELEMETRY-BEARING rather than network-free, asserted against a synthetic silent package, because silence about telemetry cannot be read as an absence of telemetry. Remaining: there is no PROFILE concept to select a no-network deployment with, so the verdict is computed and never consulted at deployment time; and the host does not yet refuse a remote destination on the strength of this verdict, so the check exists without an enforcement point.

Input is measured and admitted against explicit budgets before work begins, and over-budget input is REJECTED with the ACTUAL LIMITS - a caller told only "too large" cannot choose a smaller input. No code path truncates: the decision type has no trimmed variant and a test asserts the shape rather than trusting the absence. Every exceeded budget is reported rather than only the first, so a caller fixing one limit is not then refused for another it could have fixed at the same time. An UNMEASURED budget is skipped rather than assumed satisfied, so omitting a measurement cannot pass a check it did not undergo. The HTTP transport already measures request bytes DURING the read rather than after it, since buffering an unbounded body to measure it defeats the limit. Remaining: admission is not yet wired into the tool invocation path, so the budgets are enforced where they are called and not automatically for every request; decoding, tokenization and provider-response bounds are declared as budget kinds but nothing measures them yet; and postprocessing is unbounded.

planPreparation computes the pre-approval disclosure the requirement asks for: total download bytes, total storage bytes stated SEPARATELY because an operator approving bandwidth is not thereby approving disk, the pinned license terms surfaced BEFORE the download, and whether any asset is executable. Prebuilt engine downloads count as executable installation, and the plan flags requiresExecutableApproval when any asset is executable, so an engine download cannot ride along with a model download under one approval. The DeploymentIdentity type pins every field the requirement names: model revision, engine/SDK version, quantization, tokenizer, preprocessing recipe, plus asset hashes and source and license metadata on the plan. Remaining: NOTHING PRODUCES A PLAN YET. The catalog carries no asset locks, so no real deployment has a plan computed for it, and the requirement that the disclosure happen BEFORE approval is unexercised because there is no approval flow. Asset hashes are declared on PlannedAsset but no lock file populates them.

A VERIFIED ATOMIC ACQUISITION PATH now exists, which is the gap recorded in the previous round. Bytes are written to a temporary SIBLING of the final path, verified against the pinned digest, and only then renamed into place - a sibling because a rename within one directory is atomic and one across filesystems is not. A file at the final path is therefore either absent or complete and correct. ATOMICITY IS PROVEN AGAINST A REAL FILESYSTEM, not only against an in-memory store: a test asserts the asset directory holds exactly the content-addressed file after success, and holds only a dot-prefixed partial after a truncated transfer. The in-memory tests prove the call sequence; only the real one proves the rename. A DIGEST MISMATCH DISCARDS THE BYTES and reports NOT retryable, because a retry resuming from bytes already known to be wrong would reach the same mismatch. A transport failure is reported RETRYABLE and keeps the partial, so a caller can tell a flaky network from a corrupt asset - that distinction is the whole value of the retryable flag. RESUMABILITY HAS A DOCUMENTED PRECONDITION: it is attempted only when the source declares it can serve byte ranges, because resuming against a full-response source would APPEND a whole copy and produce bytes that hash wrong for a reason that looks like corruption. A test asserts the restart path, and another asserts a resumed transfer joins correctly and verifies the JOINED bytes. Assets are content-addressed by digest, which is what makes sharing between owners safe, and a cancelled transfer leaves a verifiable partial that is never at the final path. Remaining: transfers happen in bounded chunks and the store interface is injected, but no CONCRETE network source or on-disk store implementation ships, so acquisition is exercised entirely through injected fakes. Ownership records are computed by purgeCandidates but nothing PERSISTS them. There is no end-user-machine build step to disable, which satisfies that clause only because nothing is built at all.

The eight-state set is implemented exactly as named: unavailable, needs-preparation, preparing, prepared-cold, loading, ready, busy, failed. READINESS AND RESIDENCY ARE NOW SEPARATE QUESTIONS, which corrects a real defect in this repository: admitsInvocation previously required a deployment to be LOADED before it was callable, so a prepared-but-cold model made its tool uncallable and the tool surface flickered on every warm/cold transition - the exact outcome the requirement forbids. Callability now follows PREPARATION: prepared-cold, loading, busy and ready are all callable, while unavailable, needs-preparation and failed are not. Residency controls ADMISSION instead - immediate, loads-first or queued - which is the half it legitimately governs, and a second call to a loading deployment QUEUES rather than starting a second load of the same deployment. summarize() no longer reports a cold deployment as preparing, because that would tell an operator to wait for something that already works, and it now treats unavailable as faulted alongside failed. descriptionMayVaryWithResidency() exists and returns false, so the prohibition is asserted rather than merely intended. Remaining: nothing yet DRIVES these transitions - there is no preparation or loading lifecycle, so the states are exercised by test rather than produced by a real deployment, and no warm/cold evidence exists because no model has been loaded twice.

A DeploymentCoordinator implements single-flight preparation and loading per EXACT provider deployment, with tests that COUNT loader invocations: the single-flight test asserts the loader ran exactly once for three concurrent callers, because a coordinator that started two loads of a 349 MB model would pass every other assertion while doubling memory, and only a count catches that. The deployment key includes every identity field - extension, model, revision, engine version, quantization, tokenizer and preprocessing recipe - and a test mutates each one to assert it changes the key. Quantization is the sharpest case: the same model at int8 and fp16 produce different outputs, so loading one must not satisfy a request for the other. Reference counting is implemented and enforced: unloading a busy deployment is REFUSED and reports how many callers are using it, because unloading there would discard their work. Release is idempotent so a double release cannot corrupt the count, and revocation is the one case permitted to discard a busy deployment, explicitly and only on request. Cancellation is PER INVOCATION: a cancelled caller gives up while the deployment stays loaded and available to others, asserted by a test where a cancelled and an uncancelled caller share one load and only one is rejected. Killing the deployment on one caller cancellation would destroy another legitimate work, which the requirement forbids. WIRING WAS ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED, and the reason is worth recording. Routing provider.load() through the coordinator at the bridge moved loading AHEAD of path authorization, so a call with a denied path loaded roughly 349 MB of weights before refusing; the existing deny-before-load test failed at 9.4 seconds and caught it. The coordinator therefore remains a tested standalone component whose correct place is INSIDE an implementation load path, after the checks that must precede a load. Wiring it at the bridge would have traded a security property for a resource optimisation. Remaining: no implementation uses the coordinator yet, so it is exercised by test rather than by a real load; the catalog does not carry model revision, engine version, quantization, tokenizer or recipe, so those key components are recorded as unpinned, which is honest but means two genuinely different builds would currently share a key.

Cancellation is reported as an OUTCOME rather than a boolean claim: either the work stopped and released its resources, or it could not be interrupted safely and will run to completion with its result discarded. A test asserts the second case never reports stopped, because RES-06 forbids claiming cancellation while uncontrolled work continues indefinitely - which is also why the requirement prefers isolating an uninterruptible backend in an owned worker. Existing propagation is real where it exists: the caller abort signal reaches adapters, the invocation context carries it, the stdio bridge translates notifications/cancelled into a per-request abort without cancelling a request sharing the bridge, and closing an HTTP SSE response is specified to cancel that request. Remaining: the signal reaches inference but NOT file reads, HTTP fetches or queues, which do not exist as interruptible operations; nothing isolates an uninterruptible backend in an owned worker because there is no worker runtime; and no cancellation latency has been measured, so the duration for which cancelled work actually continues is unknown.

Memory admission reports ENFORCED and ESTIMATED figures SEPARATELY, and states what the enforced figure actually covers: process-tree, worker, v8-heap-only or none. The specific mistake the requirement names is guarded by a test: a V8 heap cap is NOT treated as a process-tree cap, because the heap bounds JavaScript objects and says nothing about native memory an inference engine allocates outside it. boundsProcessTree returns false for a heap-only scope and true only for process-tree. A null enforced figure is representable, so "nothing is enforced" is distinguishable from "enforced at zero". Remaining: nothing MEASURES peak process or worker memory, so the estimate is predicted rather than measured and `measured` is always false; no pool bound or input bound is derived from these figures; and there is no worker runtime for a worker-scoped cap to apply to.

A foreground invocation is modelled as an OUTCOME rather than a job: completed, failed, cancelled, or DISCONNECTED with a flag for whether work may have run. Disconnected is distinct from failed because there is no result to report, and distinct from completed because the call may have run. REPLAY AFTER RECONNECT IS NEVER PERMITTED, asserted rather than assumed: a call that may already have run is not safely repeatable, because its effects could be billed or delivered twice. A retry is a new request with fresh authorization and budget. Ambiguous completion is reported whenever work may have started, so a client can tell a call that never began from one that completed and whose response was lost. Cancellation on the originating stream already exists for stdio, where notifications/cancelled aborts exactly the referenced request, and the HTTP transport is specified to cancel a request when its SSE response closes. Remaining: there is no HTTP SSE response stream, so closing one cannot cancel a request in practice; there are no server deadlines; and legacy HTTP session-disconnect semantics are absent only because there is no legacy handling at all.

All eight budget kinds are declared and independently enforced: source-bytes, decoded-pixels, audio-samples, video-seconds, video-frames, processor-tokens, batch and output-vectors. The product defaults are the ones the requirement states verbatim: 8 MiB and 16 megapixels for an image, 120 seconds, 32 frames and 128 MiB for video. A test asserts each number, because a default that drifts silently is a limit nobody agreed to. Budgets are enforced INDEPENDENTLY, proven by a 200-second video under the byte cap still being refused for its duration. NO SILENT SAMPLING: coverage is returned with every result, naming whether the source was fully processed, how many units were, and the sampling instruction that was applied. Incomplete coverage WITHOUT an instruction is reported as a defect rather than dressed up as policy. Decompression bombs are rejected on the DECLARED expanded size before allocation, because a check that runs after decompression has already lost. Remaining: the decoder-process bound and the actual decoded-pixel measurement are not implemented, since nothing decodes an image or video on this host; the requirement that defaults stay below the SELECTED model constraints is unenforced because no model is selected at admission time; and model context limits that may force lower admission are not consulted.

The initial per-leaf maxima are implemented and each is asserted INDIVIDUALLY - one provider attempt, no automatic repair, 60 seconds, 1024 output tokens, two image inputs - because a budget that drifts silently is a limit nobody agreed to. NARROWING ONLY EVER LOWERS: every figure takes the minimum, so a caller asking for more than the profile permits receives the profile figure. A test asserts a request for 9999 seconds yields 60. A nullable limit is narrowed the same way, and a local-only profile cannot be widened to permit remote destinations by any request. A repair is permitted only when a reviewed profile explicitly allowed one AND the same ROOT deadline still has time, because a repair consuming a fresh deadline would evade the budget rather than fit inside it. UNKNOWN COST STAYS UNKNOWN. The monetary figure has three states - a known amount, unknown with a reason - and a test asserts the unknown form contains no zero, because reporting it as zero presents a call that may be billed as free, which is the failure the requirement names. A local-only profile prohibits remote destinations INDEPENDENTLY of how the tool was implemented, since the check asks the budget rather than the implementation. Remaining: no GRANT supplies these budgets, so nothing sets model-call, token or image maxima from a server grant; the budgets are not enforced at an invocation site, only computable; and no monetary accounting is performed, so a known cost is representable but never produced.

The prohibition is now mechanically checked rather than conventional: the architecture gate rejects an extension that imports the host package by path, imports DSH, or climbs out of its own package with a relative import, and it runs over both shipped extensions as part of `npm run verify`. Both extensions import only @try-works/tool-mode-extension-sdk, with the vendor model packages reached through a dynamic import at load time rather than a static dependency. Remaining: the check covers the packages in this repository and would not see a third-party extension published elsewhere; enforcing it for those needs a packaging-time check on the consumer side.

Every extension is deactivatable through the same path, a built-in being a first-party package rather than an exception. Individual tools toggle independently of activation: disabling one tool leaves the package active and its other tools callable, and toggling an unknown tool is refused rather than ignored. Uninstall is implemented for third-party packages with the EXTENSION_IN_USE gate. Remaining: BUILTIN_PROTECTED is unreachable because nothing is marked built-in yet, and asset purging does not exist.

requirements.summary: One model or executor can supply several tools.

requirements.evidence: stagedInstall returns `activation: "inactive"` as an explicit field so a caller cannot mistake a successful install for a usable tool, and it imports nothing: the test fixture ships an entry that THROWS on import, so reaching the assertions proves installation never executed it. No inference, no warming, no tool or skill publication. Remaining: no inventory and no activation path, so the state an install produces is not yet persisted or readable.

The ordered pipeline runs and now RECORDS its result: fetch into a unique quarantine directory -> verify SHA-512 -> list entries -> validate the entry list -> extract -> discover as data -> promote by atomic rename -> record in the store lock -> remove quarantine on every path. Recording happens AFTER the bytes are in place, because a lock entry naming a directory that does not exist would make verification report a missing installation as a changed one. Remaining: dependency resolution and locking, the permission/licence/platform preview, and operator approval are not implemented.

Entry-list validation refuses traversal, absolute paths, drive letters, UNC, backslashes, NUL bytes, Windows reserved device names, segments ending in a dot or space, duplicates, Windows case collisions, symlinks and hardlinks, plus entry-count, per-entry, total-byte and expansion-ratio bounds. Tested against REAL zip archives built at the byte level, because adm-zip sanitizes entry names on write and therefore cannot produce the hostile archives these defenses exist to refuse; a raw ZIP writer in the test suite supplies the bytes. The extractor re-asserts confinement at the write, so a bypassed validator still cannot escape. Remaining: fetch time limits are passed through but not enforced by the SDK, which owns no network stack.

discoverExtension reads package.json and the manifest as BOUNDED data (256 KB / 512 KB limits) and never imports the entry: the test fixture writes an entry that throws on import, and reaching the assertions proves it never ran. It enforces name, version, type:module, an explicit exports map, the toolMode.manifest field, containment of the manifest path, and rejects malformed or oversized JSON as INVALID_EXTENSION. Remaining: quarantine fetch, archive inspection and the install/activate lifecycle are not implemented.

extension-manifest-1.1.0.schema.json ships with the SDK and is enforced at runtime via Ajv 2020-12. Beyond the schema it checks exact id/version agreement with the package, unique local ids per contribution kind, duplicate caller-facing tool NAMES reported as TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT, referenced files that must exist, paths that must not escape the package, and unknown REQUIRED features blocking activation as INCOMPATIBLE_PROTOCOL. Unknown top-level fields are rejected while the x- vendor namespace is admitted. Remaining: asset-lock validation (EXT-15) and keyed digests.

A 1.0 manifest is normalized to module execution as a VIEW, leaving the input object untouched so the recorded digest still describes the installed bytes; the lift provenance is attached after validation rather than smuggled past the closed schema. Protocol 1.1.0, runtime API major 1, and the five separate identities are documented in code. Remaining: minor-version conformance tests and the contract/recipe/model revision separation are not implemented end to end.

requirements.summary: Publish the SDK and reference host.
requirements.evidence: The SDK now defines and exports the complete public runtime API: ToolModeExtensionV1, ExtensionContextV1, ExtensionInstanceV1, ModelProviderV1, ProviderInspectionV1, PreparedAssetMapV1, InvocationContextV1, JsonObject/JsonValue, the DisposeReason vocabulary, defineExtension() which rejects a wrong apiVersion at the declaration site, and the reserved-meta guard. Loading is implemented in load.ts: the entry is resolved from the package own exports map rather than a convention, the shape is validated BEFORE create() runs, and a missing dispose() is refused because a host with no way to release an instance could never fully stop it. Remaining: the declarative interpreter, the conformance helpers, and the reference test host with a fake harness broker are not implemented, and the SDK is not published to npm.

All five named context contracts exist with the required semantics documented: ExtensionContextV1 carries host-issued identity, private storage, a bounded logger and a teardown signal, and deliberately NO DSH ctx, registry mutation, global credentials or unfiltered environment; ProviderInspectionV1 reports readiness/features/missing/runtimeVersion and inspection is implemented to read only approved local state (a test asserts it reports unprepared before a load rather than claiming ready); PreparedAssetMapV1 and InvocationContextV1 carry verified handles and call-scoped grants with no caller-supplied authority. Remaining: the asset map is a type without a host implementation, and the file/network broker operations are typed but have no enforcing host behind them.

Import and create() are lightweight and tested: the extension declares no assets because Tongue bundles its weights, module import performs no work, and a test asserts createProvider returns a handle in well under a second rather than parsing the weight file, with inspect() reporting unprepared until load() is called. Disposal is idempotent and the host disposes providers per model and instances per extension. Remaining: there is no pooling, no concurrency admission, and unload() is only a cache drop because no provider holds a process-level resource yet.

Publication is built WHOLE and consulted before anything is registered. buildSurface produces a complete surface from the candidates, the host registers a tool only when that surface actually published it, and an incoherent surface is refused rather than partially applied. The rules EXT-24 states absolutely are enforced and tested: a tool without a runnable implementation binding is withheld (no-implementation) because a schema alone is a promise nothing can keep; a FAILED deployment is withheld with the reason that waiting will not help; an UNPREPARED model publishes readiness and a preparation skill but NOT a working inference tool; a USAGE skill is withheld unless every tool it requires is visible, naming the missing tool; duplicate tool names are REFUSED rather than silently resolved, because a name identifies one tool; and every withholding is reported with a code, subject and owner rather than dropped silently. The surface carries a generation and swaps as a whole through one callback receiving both sides, so a consumer never infers the change from a partially-updated view. Skill provenance is tracked: orphanedSkills names the skills whose owning extension is gone. Remaining: DSH tool declarations, MCP discovery and Code Mode type discovery are not yet updated from the generation - only the host tool registration consults it - and readiness is currently always "ready" for a runnable model because no preparation lifecycle exists, so the needs-preparation path is proven by test rather than by a real deployment.

The six dimensions are modelled separately and now PERSIST: a profile state file round-trips installation, desired and observed activation, per-deployment readiness, per-profile tool selection with the selected implementation, and export authorization independently, with profiles kept apart. A corrupt or oversized file, or one malformed entry, invalidates the whole file rather than dropping just the bad part, because a file that is demonstrably untrustworthy must not activate anything. Remaining: activation does not yet write these states, so persistence is exercised by tests rather than by a lifecycle operation.

Activation verifies the installed bytes and locks BEFORE publishing anything (a package edited after installation is refused as INTEGRITY_MISMATCH with nothing published), persists intended-active before publication so a crash leaves a record rather than a silent no-op, publishes every required contribution through an injected registrar, and commits the catalog generation ONLY once all of them were accepted. A failed registration rolls back narrowly: only the handles this activation published are withdrawn, the generation does not advance, and a healthy extension stays active AND callable - tested with one good and one failing package in the same profile. Readiness is assessed rather than assumed: merely unprepared assets activate with needs-preparation diagnostics as EXT-26 requires, while a FAILED deployment refuses activation because it will not become ready by waiting. Remaining: no managed worker is started and the public entry/API is not validated, because there is no worker runtime; provider handles are not created.

Deactivation persists inactive intent before withdrawing, withdraws contributions, and refuses to claim a full stop when it cannot confirm one. A NEW CASE was found while writing the CLI tests: a fresh process (or a CLI not attached to the host) holds no publication handles, so it cannot withdraw another process's contributions. It previously reported a clean stop in that situation, which is the exact lie EXT-27 forbids. The lifecycle now detects an extension recorded as active while this instance holds no handles and reports the cleanup failure with guidance to stop the owning host, leaving the state quarantined. Remaining: active calls are not cancelled, disposal hooks are not called, no grace period is joined, and no owned process is terminated, because there is no worker runtime.

Uninstalling an active package returns EXTENSION_IN_USE unless deactivation is explicitly requested, and the CLI now prints the impact preview (affected profile and each contributed tool) before refusing, as EXT-28 requires. With --deactivate the deactivation sequence runs first, the record is removed, the disabled tombstone is RETAINED so nothing silently resurrects the package, and --purge-assets reports that deletion may complete after restart on Windows. Remaining: private resolved dependencies are not deleted, credential references and executable-content approvals are not revoked, and BUILTIN_PROTECTED is not reachable because nothing is marked built-in.

The full required command family exists and runs as `dsh-tool-mode`: extensions list|inspect|install|activate|prepare|deactivate|uninstall and tools enable|disable, with --store, --profile and --integrity. The logic is a library entry taking argv and an output sink, so the REFUSAL paths are tested as directly as the happy ones rather than being left to manual checking. INSTALL REQUIRES --integrity: an install with no verifiable digest is refused, because EXT-12 makes integrity the record that later verification depends on and an unverified install cannot be undone. OFFLINE EDITS TAKE EXCLUSIVE STORE OWNERSHIP: mutating commands acquire store.lock, refuse when a live process holds it, treat a dead holder as stale rather than blocking forever, and release only their own lock. Uninstall of an active extension refuses and shows the impact preview (profiles and tools) before naming --deactivate. Deactivation that cannot confirm a full stop reports a quarantine rather than a clean result. Remaining: there is no running-host management channel, so commands act offline only; the management surface is deliberately absent from the inference tool surface as EXT-31 requires, but the settings actions and the MCP-side management grant do not exist.

Discovery now exposes public extension/implementation provenance and readiness per model, through the real tool pipeline: contract, extension package, modelId inside that package, the tool name actually published, and the alternatives not selected, plus a readiness value and a callable flag. An ABSENT tool is explicable rather than merely missing - a model that cannot run on this host reports callable false, and a withheld contribution reports its surface code and message. The shape is TOTAL: every row carries every field, including for a model with no contract or extension binding, so a caller never handles a partially-populated model. One helper computes the publication decision for both the installer and discovery, because two call sites computing it separately is how a tool gets registered while discovery reports it withheld. The listing discloses no filesystem layout or approved roots.
