Remaining: tool_mode_list and tool_mode_describe themselves are not created - this extends the existing model_tools surface - external callers are not yet filtered to authorized information, the model_tools migration is not documented, and no management grant exists for installer/update/uninstall bindings.

The store now RECORDS what it installs: an operator-owned extensions.lock.json holds complete resolved source/identity records (identity, version, install path, archive digest, CONTENT digest, source, timestamp), so identity survives restart and a package edited on disk after installation is detected before activation rather than trusted. Version-keyed layout keeps two versions side by side. Corrupted state FAILS CLOSED: a lock or profile file that cannot be trusted yields NO records and a diagnostic, never a fallback to "everything installed is active", and a lock that could not be read is refused as an append target rather than silently overwritten. All writes are atomic (temp plus rename) and a failed write throws instead of reporting success. Remaining: per-install dependency locks and transaction records are not implemented, and cleanup-pending tombstones do not exist.

All 15 published codes exist with the operation, safe recovery advice and a retryable flag DERIVED from the code so a permission refusal cannot be mistaken for a transient fault. Recovery text is passed through a sanitiser that strips credential- and path-shaped spans. Remaining: the codes are not yet raised by install/activate/uninstall, which do not exist.

Invocation receipts and lifecycle records exist as SEPARATE structures, because mixing them would let a caller reading a receipt learn about operator actions it has no business seeing and would make an audit trail indistinguishable from execution metadata. A receipt records the extension package, its version, the content digest, the dependency-lock digest, the model/recipe identity, the activation generation and the execution location; the content digest is what lets two runs of the SAME version be told apart, since a package can be replaced at one version. Receipts are emitted on every SUCCESSFUL call and NOT on a refused one, because a receipt for a call that failed validation would claim provenance for a result nobody received; verified through the real pipeline, including that the invoked text never appears in a receipt. The metadata-only rule is enforced by CONSTRUCTION: buildInvocationReceipt takes only host-resolved inputs, so there is no parameter through which a body, token or skill text could arrive, and every warning passes a redactor that strips npm/GitHub/bearer tokens and absolute paths of either shape. redactPath reduces a path to its leaf plus a short digest, so an operator can correlate two receipts without learning the filesystem layout. Lifecycle records carry the operation, outcome, profile and approving principal, refuse an operator approval with no identity, and carry no execution fields. The log policy defaults to quiet, metadata-only, telemetry off, and REFUSES an undeclared network origin rather than logging it. Remaining: receipts are retained in a bounded in-memory ring, not persisted to a receipt store; lifecycle records are built but not yet emitted by the CLI or the lifecycle; the store still records no dependency-lock digest, so that field is always null; and extension logging is not yet driven through the policy by a real extension.

Stdio cancellation uses notifications/cancelled and aborts EXACTLY the referenced request: a test holds two requests in flight, cancels one, and asserts the first signal is aborted while the second is NOT, which is the property that stops one cancellation tearing down a shared worker. A cancellation for a request the bridge does not own is reported rather than ignored, because that usually means the client and bridge disagree about what is in flight. A JSON response channel is implemented. Remaining: no request-scoped SSE response channel, so closing an HTTP SSE response cannot cancel its request; cancellation is not translated into an HTTP abort of a request sharing a bridge or model worker in the network direction, because there is no SSE stream to close.

No resumability is implemented, and the absence is now FALSIFIABLY asserted. The evidence THIS ENTRY USED TO CITE COULD NOT FAIL: it sent Last-Event-ID and the same request without it, then compared the two bodies, but the handler never reads that header at all, so it was comparing a value WITH ITSELF and deleting the ban entirely would not have turned it red. An adversarial review found this, and the test was rebuilt with three checks, the third of which is the only kind that can prove an ABSENT feature: (1) the header changes no observable byte; (2) the response is application/json and carries no SSE `id:` field, because replay requires an event stream; (3) the header is not consulted ANYWHERE in the transport, asserted against the SOURCE with comment lines excluded, so reading-and-ignoring would fail it. The rewrite was MUTATION-TESTED: adding one line reading the header to src/mcp/http.ts turns it RED (33 pass, 1 fail) and reverting turns it green (34/34), so it now catches precisely the mutation it names. A retry remains a new request with fresh authorization.

The requirements are implemented and each has a test: stdout carries protocol traffic and NOTHING else while diagnostics go through a separate named sink, so there is no single output to confuse; the request body is forwarded VERBATIM so ids and per-request metadata cannot drift between the two hops, with the bridge regenerating only the headers; nothing is retained between requests except in-flight cancellation state keyed by request id and removed when the request settles, so one stdio process is not treated as one conversation; EOF aborts bridge-owned in-flight requests and sends nothing to the host, which is shared and not the bridge to stop; and a malformed frame is answered on the PROTOCOL channel because a client waiting for a reply would not see a diagnostic. Remaining: the executable is not run end-to-end (sandbox limitation above), and a legacy stdio translation mode is neither offered nor tested.

Catalog subscriptions are implemented and each rule the requirement states has a test. ACKNOWLEDGE FIRST AND ONLY WHAT IS SUPPORTED: the acknowledgement carries the filter the server will actually honour, not the one requested, so a client asking for four notification types and receiving one is told the truth rather than waiting forever for three that never come. A type the client did NOT request is never acknowledged, because granting one would start sending an unrequested notification. The acknowledgement is returned WITH the result, and the subscription is marked announced during listen, so no event can precede it - the ordering is enforced rather than remembered. NO EVENT BEFORE ACKNOWLEDGEMENT is proven by publishing immediately after listen and observing delivery. EVERY EVENT CARRIES THE SUBSCRIPTION ID in the revision notification metadata, without which a client holding several subscriptions cannot tell which one an event belongs to, and it carries the catalog generation so a client can distinguish a real change from a duplicate delivery. FILTER PER CALLER: each subscription is bound to one authenticated client and sees only its own catalog, delivered as one addressed message per subscriber rather than a shared broadcast whose safety would depend on how the transport iterated it. A test asserts two subscribers receive two distinct subscription ids and that a client that requested nothing receives nothing. Subscription ids are SERVER-ISSUED, because a caller-chosen id would let one client address another subscription, and closing one requires ownership. TEARDOWN IS ANNOUNCED: revoking a grant sends notifications/cancelled referencing the SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST before the subscription is removed, so a client learns its access ended rather than inferring it from a dropped stream, and there is no window in which one last event reaches a revoked client. Revoking one client leaves unrelated clients alive. P26-10 is respected by omission: the catalog stream emits only notifications/tools/list_changed, never progress or logging, which belong on the response stream of the call that produced them. Remaining: there is no SSE response stream, so a subscription is a series of messages on the request response channel rather than a long-lived event stream; resource and prompt catalog changes do not exist, so only toolsListChanged is supported and advertised.

The channel separation rule is respected and tested: the catalog subscription stream emits ONLY notifications/tools/list_changed, never progress and never logging. Progress stays on the response stream of the call that produced it, because routing it onto the catalog stream would deliver one call progress to every subscriber. Protocol logging is not adopted at all, which the revision deprecates, so there is no logging channel to conflate with model-facing results. Remaining: there is no request-scoped SSE response stream, so progress cannot actually be delivered on an originating call stream yet - the separation holds because neither channel exists rather than because two exist and are kept apart, and interleaved subscriptions with active inference calls on one client are therefore not exercised.

The revision declared TTL/cache-scope mechanism is used: cacheable results carry cacheScope private and ttlMs 0, which the pinned CacheableResult definition REQUIRES on DiscoverResult and ListToolsResult alike, asserted by test and by schema validation. Zero TTL with a private scope is the correct default for an authorization-filtered catalog: a shared cache keyed on tool names would leak one caller permitted set to another. Remaining: nothing caches yet, so the fields state the policy rather than govern a cache; authorization is not recomputed per invocation at the MCP boundary because the caller-permitted set is not yet computed there.

Static-token custom authentication is implemented and is explicitly NOT claimed as OAuth: authProfile() reports oauth21ResourceServer false with a note stating the profile is not implemented and is not claimed, and claimsOAuthConformance() returns false so a status report or compatibility matrix cannot assert otherwise by accident. Plain unauthenticated loopback is not available: every request including server/discover needs a credential. Credentials are per-client and independently revocable in the sense that each client endpoint validates its own token. Remaining: no OAuth 2.1 resource-server implementation, no protected-resource or authorization-server metadata, no audience or scope validation, no challenge flow beyond a bare WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, and no dynamic registration. P26-15 permits the static-token mode only while forbidding the conformance claim, which is the line this implementation holds.

Tested here: origin rejection, invalid and missing tokens, mixed clients with independent credentials, token leakage (a failure response is asserted not to contain either the configured token or the presented one), and header/version errors. Remaining: expired and wrong-audience tokens and insufficient scopes do not exist because there is no OAuth profile; bridge credential protection is untested because the bridge does not exist; headless operation fails with actionable guidance for a missing token but no interactive approval path exists.

A fixture corpus and a SEPARATELY AUTHORED PROBE exist. Fifteen sanitized fixtures are captured as FROZEN FILES under docs/tool-mode/fixtures/mcp-2026-07-28/, covering discovery, tool invocation (success and domain failure), header and version errors, missing metadata, an unknown tool, an unknown method, unauthenticated access, a non-loopback peer, concurrency and cancellation. Each records what it demonstrates and the expectation an auditor can check. The probe (scripts/probe-mcp-conformance.mjs) is independent by construction: it reads the frozen files from disk, imports none of the server, dispatch or protocol modules, and validates against the PINNED upstream schema with Ajv, so it cannot inherit a mistake from the code that produced the fixtures. It runs in npm run verify and reports 34 checks with 0 failures. The manifest pins the schema by immutable commit and records the official SDK version together with the note that the SDK cannot speak this revision, which is part of the MCP-04 answer. The probe found FOUR real defects on first run: two fixtures that LIED about what they demonstrated (a loopback-refusal case captured from the loopback address, and a domain-failure case that used an unpublished tool name so it recorded an invalid-params error instead), a JSON-RPC error carrying id null which the pinned RequestId type does not admit, and a mapping bug in the probe itself. What it does NOT establish is stated in the probe header: the fixtures were produced by this repository own code, so the probe shows the CAPTURED BYTES satisfy the upstream definitions, not that every possible request would. Remaining: subscription and SSE fixtures are absent because those surfaces do not exist, and the selected-SDK half of the requirement cannot be met while the official SDK cannot speak 2026-07-28 - this is an adaptation, so there is no independent SDK side to cross-check against.

verification/requirements.json now exists and maps every normative ID to its owning module, test layer, required platform, source digest and evidence, generated from the pinned spec text rather than maintained by hand, so a requirement cannot silently go missing. Building it found TWO REAL DEFECTS that had been invisible for several rounds. First, the extraction pattern was `[A-Z]{2,6}-nn`, which cannot match a family containing digits, so the ENTIRE section 20 family (P26-01..P26-17) was absent from the inventory and from the traceability matrix. The count of normative requirements was 210 and is actually 227. Second, two status keys named requirements that DO NOT EXIST: MCP-14 and MCP-17, recorded in rounds 16 and 22. The MCP family ends at MCP-13, and the requirements actually meant were section 20 P26-14 (discovery caching) and P26-17 (verification artifacts). Both keys are corrected and the evidence moved with them, because the judgements were sound and only the labels were wrong. What surfaced both was this requirement: an inventory of every normative ID immediately shows status keys matching nothing, which is exactly what mapping every ID is for. Remaining: owning modules are inferred from the requirement family rather than declared per requirement, so a requirement implemented outside its family nominal module would be mis-attributed; test IDs are not yet linked to individual requirement IDs, which the requirement asks for; and the explicit proposed-spec-change mechanism for altering a requirement is not implemented.

The mandated statuses PASS, FAIL, BLOCKED, NOT_RUN and NOT_APPLICABLE are the only ones the evidence generator emits, and tests assert the no-false-pass rules directly. A requirement that is PARTIAL is reported as FAIL at the test level and NEVER as PASS, because PARTIAL is work that does not meet its stated outcome; a BLOCKED requirement is reported as BLOCKED and never as PASS or NOT_RUN; and a requirement with no recorded status is NOT_RUN, since treating "we did not test it" as "it passed" is the same false pass in a quieter form. The release gate exits nonzero while any mandatory gate is not PASS and reports what that means, and its RED state is asserted by a test that runs it and requires a nonzero exit. The gate is deliberately SEPARATE from npm run verify: the dev loop asks whether the code does what its tests say, while the release gate asks whether the product may be released. Collapsing them would make one of the two lie - either the dev loop would fail for reasons unrelated to the change at hand, or the release gate would report a readiness that does not exist. Remaining: the generator does not itself require a reviewed reason for a NOT_APPLICABLE status; it emits that status but nothing yet enforces that one was reviewed.

requirements.evidence: verification/evidence.json records, per run: the git commit and branch, whether the working tree was DIRTY (because evidence gathered against a dirty tree describes a state that exists in no commit and cannot be reproduced from the commit alone), the platform and Node version, the execution command, the installed package identities, a timestamp, and per-requirement status and evidence text. The requirement to store no secrets or private media is met by construction: the generator reads only the spec text, the status record and package manifests, none of which contain either. Remaining: fixture and artifact hashes are not recorded; there is no path to bounded sanitized logs; red and green runs are not linked to distinct source states because only one run is recorded at a time; and no CI artifact exists to strengthen provenance.

verification/RELEASE-REPORT.md is generated with the sections the requirement names: installed package identities, requirement status by TDD-06 category, the MCP conformance matrix, the model and modality support matrix, known limitations and unresolved gates, and reproduction instructions. The MCP matrix records FACTS rather than a version string - the pinned schema commit, and that the official SDK does NOT support the revision - because the requirement warns that a report whose only protocol assertion is a string equality for 2026-07-28 fails the gate. The report states what it does NOT claim, and the model matrix marks Tongue and Voz as extracted and tested but NOT yet run against real inference, which is the distinction most easily lost in a status summary. Remaining: there is no custom-author demonstration and no migration-effects section, because a third-party author has not yet packaged an extension; measurements are absent because no memory or latency qualification has been run; and reproducibility from a clean checkout is asserted rather than exercised, since no clean-checkout run has been performed.
